newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian government brings in more liberal reformers.
newsitem.headline: Russian government brings in more liberal reformers.

text.p: Russia's new government brought in more liberal reformers in the latest stage of a long reshuffle on Wednesday.
Announcing two new ministerial appointments, Pime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said the government's main and immediate target was to bring about economic growth and revive investment.
"This is the task already for the current year," he told a news conference after a meeting with President Boris Yeltsin to map the way forward and approve the latest cabinet appointees.

Chernomyrdin -- flanked by his youthful and reformist new first deputy prime minsters, Anatoly Chubais, 41, and Boris Nemtsov, 37, who were appointed earlier this month -- stressed the need to begin radical structural reforms among companies, monopolies, housing and welfare.

Maintaining the liberal tone of Yeltsin's reshaped team, Chernomyrdin said former economy minister Yevgeny Yasin, the guiding spirit of many of Russia's economic reforms would become a minister without portfolio.
Yasin, an economics professor with long experience, had been expected to stay an influential figure behind the scenes.
Chernomyrdin said he would deal with economic questions, including coordinating government programmes and analysing them.
He said Alexei Kudrin, another Chubais ally, was being appointed First Deputy Finance Minister. Chubais himself holds the finance portfolio.
The prime minister said a new approach to budget and tax policy was needed.
"Without changes in the tax system we will not be able to consider a budget for 1998," he said, adding that tax collection remained extremely difficult in March.
Chubais said revenue was Russia's "hottest and most acute problem at the moment" and changes were urgently needed.
He said Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov would retain day-to-day charge of Russia's tax and customs services.

But foreign trade activities and policy-making in the tax and customs services would be the responsibity of Alfred Kokh, another deputy prime minister who deals with privatisation and who is close to Chubais.
Yeltsin met his three most senior ministers earlier on Wednesday on the eve of planned protests against massive wage arrears.
His government has its work cut out to convince Russians that it can resolve the non-payments crisis which has left millions of workers and pensioners struggling to make ends meet.
Workers are owed over 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back wages, of which the state owes 10 trillion and many people have not been paid for months.
Trade unions say up to 20 million people will strike or take part in demonstrations during Thursday's day of protests against the arrears, but others are expected to work normally.
